messages.subject: Too flexible SPDE in a spatial poisson model?
parts:
Dear INLA group,

we are developing a predictive spatial  poission model of deer,
using a combination of spatial and other covariates. We are assuming an SPDE-type spatial effect.
Fitting the model results in a very good R2 between predicted and observed deer counts. 

However, when we compare the prediction of the fixed effects only, removing the spatial effect, the R2 becomes incredibly low, on the order of 0.01 (see also the attached plot of predicted VS true deercount when including and excluding the spatial effect).  In comparison, a simple poisson regression excluding random effects gets an R2 of 0.06 - still not brilliant, but definitely better than the result of the INLA model. 

My guess is that the spde is "too flexible", exactly following the observed counts with no remaining variation to fit the other covariates to. Would this be a reasonable interpretation, and if so, how would you go about fixing it? After reading previous posts on here relating to SPDE models,  I've played around with the alpha, which doesn't affect anything, and with prior.variance.nominal. Prior.variance.nominal does do something, in that when it's set to 10^-7 or so, the SPDE becomes very slowly varying; but any lower than that, and the estimated random effects become "exact" again. A model without the SPDE leads to R2's of 0.25 or so...
Another approach I've been thinking about is to make the grid coarser, thereby forcing inla to average the effect of multiple data points, but I'm not if this is sensible. 


On a tangential note, I am painfully aware that using R2 for model diagnostics on a spatial predictive poisson model is terribly abusive - any suggestions for better ways of evaluating/reporting model fit and predictive performance would be much appreciated!


Best regards,
Gustaf


Code here:
----------
##Hull and mesh
prdomain2 <- inla.nonconvex.hull(coords2, convex= -0.05, resolution=c(100,100)) ## Changing convex gives more or less bendy boundary
mesh4<- inla.mesh.2d(boundary=prdomain2,
loc=points,
cutoff=10000,
offset=c(3000, 10000),
max.edge=c(15000, 100000) ) ## Change maxedge to get bigger/smaller resolution
plot(mesh4)
points2 <- cbind(rd2$E,rd2$N)
points(points2[,1], points2[,2], pch=19, cex=.5, col="red")

##Setting up the spde model

deerdens.spde2 = inla.spde2.matern(mesh=mesh4,
alpha=2,
prior.variance.nominal = 10^(-exp),
prior.range.nominal =NULL ##priors here can/should be tweaked to adjust how bendable the random fields is.

)
A.est = inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh4, loc=coords2)

#use the inla.stack function
spde.index2 = inla.spde.make.index(name="spatial.field", n.spde=deerdens.spde2$n.spde)

#note random effcts have to be listed in covars here

effects = list(c(list(intercept=rep(1,deerdens.spde2$n.spde)),spde.index2),
covar=data.all[,c("ALL.ROADS", "ELEVATION", "ELEV.TRI", "ASPECT", "ASPECT.TRI", 
"P.GRASS", "P.MIXEDF", "annualNDVI_grass",
"avSlopeGreenUp_grass", "annualNDVI_mixedforest", 
"avSlopeGreenUp_mixedforest", "DEER.COUNT.TYPE", "YEAR")])

Hi Gustaf,

If I understand you correctly, you want to penalise the complexity of the spde model. We have a new prior meant to do this, which has been successful in a couple of cases. I attach code for it here.

Note: I would not say "the spde is too flexible",I would say "we use priors for the hyper-parameters that represents too flexible models". But maybe this is what you mean.



local.inla.spde2.matern.new = function(mesh, alpha=2, prior.pc.rho, prior.pc.sig)
{
  # Call inla.spde2.matern with range and standard deviation parametrization
  d = INLA:::inla.ifelse(inherits(mesh, "inla.mesh"), 2, 1)
  nu = alpha-d/2
  kappa0 = log(8*nu)/2
  tau0   = 0.5*(lgamma(nu)-lgamma(nu+d/2)-d/2*log(4*pi))-nu*kappa0
  spde   = inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh,
                             B.tau   = cbind(tau0,   nu,  -1),
                             B.kappa = cbind(kappa0, -1, 0))
  
  # Change prior information
  param = c(prior.pc.rho, prior.pc.sig)
  spde$f$hyper.default$theta1$prior = "pcspdega"
  spde$f$hyper.default$theta1$param = param
  spde$f$hyper.default$theta1$initial = log(prior.pc.rho[1])+1
  spde$f$hyper.default$theta2$initial = log(prior.pc.sig[1])-1
  
  # End and return
  return(invisible(spde))  
}


# And then call the function with
sig0 = 1; rho0 = .3 #rho0 is typical range, sig0 typical sd
# - YOU MUST SET rho0 , e.g. to half the length/width of your space
# - You may reduce sig0 to have less spatial effect
# - You may increase rho0 additionally, to make the spatial effect smoother

spde = local.inla.spde2.matern.new(mesh, prior.pc.rho = c(rho0, 0.5), prior.pc.sig = c(sig0, 0.5))

# Taking out the spde
If you have fitted the model with the spde, it is a bit difficult to "take out" the spde part and only think about the rest. This is because the (posterior) distribution of the spatial field is heavily correlated with the distributions of the fixed betas (in cases where you have spatial covariates). (I.e. feel free to do it, but be careful with interpretation)

Example: The spatial field is sometimes heavily confounded with the intercept, but for predictions, this does not matter at all, since they are integrated out jointly.

# Suggestions for evaluating the model
In sample: 
- R2 with median posterior, for checing mean fit
- Check how many of the points fall inside 95% credible intervals (marginally), for checking "uncertainty fit"
- dic, waic (for checking Bayesian model fitness)

Out of sample:
- cpo (may take some time though) (for checking marginal out-of-sample fit, mean and uncertainty)
- hold-out sets (corresponding to your desired "prediction scenarios")

# code in the inla call
... control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, cpo=TRUE, waic = TRUE) ...

# More
I tried to answer your main questions. I hope you will ask further questions, or restate the ones you are the most interested in :)


Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

Hi Haakon and the INLA help group,

This is a bit of a delayed response following summer vacations and a renewed stab at making sense of this project. 
First, thanks a lot for pointing me in the direction of the PC prior. It was a fair bit easier to make sense of than the previous parametrisations. 
I've now spent a good amount of time experimenting with different values for Rho and sigma, and investigating how the resulting model fit behaves.
Unfortunately, the results are still troublesome. 

Basically, I can make the model flip between having a covariate effect and a completely flat SPDE, and zero covariate effects with a SPDE that fits the observations near perfectly.  The only intermediate I’ve found is one where the spade is on the order of [0.99,1.01], i.e. plus or minus ~1 percent. Which is too small to have any real effect. 

What bothers me is that I can’t understand how this solution can give a higher likelihood value than one which incorporates both covariates and SPDE. A regular regression type model  without side gives a fit that is, if not good, then at least explaining some of the variation in the observations, and the SPDE should then be able to take up the slack. It “feels” like incorporation the information inherent in the covariates should always lower the likelihood...

I've attached the code to this mail, in case anyone feels like having a look and see if we are making any glaringly obvious mistakes. 
Alternatively, is there a different spatial model apart from the SPDE approach you would suggest as being a potential alternative? 

All the best and thanks in advance,
Gustaf

parts:
There are two different log-scales here:
1) loglinear predictor
2) internal log representation of the parameters.

For 1), yes, you need to think of the prior for sigma in terms of its effect on the logscsle of the loglinear predictor. But thats unrelated to issue 2). With pcmatern, the parameters are specified in the range&sigma scaled, regardless of how it may be represented internally.

For pcmatern, as should already be clear from ?inla.spde.pcmatern,
for range 200, use 200, not log(200)
for sigma, consider the sensible variability on the log of the Poisson expectation.

One possibility is to consider the standard deviation on the expectation scale, pick the desired quantile from that, and convert that to the sigma parameter in a lognormal distribution to use in the pcmatern definition. (But this is not necessarily more intuitive than considering sigma directly...)

Finn
